strengths: UniAP addresses a useful infrastructure problem: jointly choosing pipeline placement and DP/TP/FSDP strategies under communication and memory constraints. Its application to ViT and Swin establishes relevance to computer vision.

Table 2 reports meaningful measured gains. On EnvB, ViT throughput reaches 45.58 samples/s versus 38.74 for Alpa and 32.20 for Galvatron; Swin improves from 13.90 to 19.08 samples/s. UniAP also successfully trains Swin on EnvA where Galvatron encounters OOM.

Strategy optimization is substantially faster in the reported experiments, including approximately 11–17 times faster than Galvatron for several EnvA workloads. Finding equally effective strategies faster is valuable even where training throughput ties the baseline.

The evaluation covers five Transformer models and several hardware configurations. The reported 3.59% average throughput-estimation error supports the cost model on the selected configurations, while the hardware specifications, solver settings, and placement case study provide useful implementation context.
weaknesses: The stated placement constraints have a consequential correctness gap. Equations (6a–c) enforce contiguity but do not order pipeline stages. For a graph u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies these constraints and the placement constraints, yet Equation (4) assigns zero communication cost because it counts only edges from stage j to j+1. The optimizer can therefore prefer an undercosted placement. Appendix A proves contiguity only and does not resolve this problem.

The advertised MIQP formulation is incomplete as written. Equations (3) and (4) contain fourth-degree products of placement and strategy-selection variables, such as Pui·Pvi·Suk·Svl. Auxiliary-variable reformulations are possible, but none is supplied. This is a correctable specification issue, yet it prevents reproduction of the central solver formulation and leaves its relationship to the reported implementation unclear.

The repeated optimality claims exceed the evidence. Appendix D permits termination after 15 seconds with a gap below 4% and imposes a 60-second limit; achieved gaps and timeout frequencies are not reported. Moreover, optimality of an estimated objective within the enumerated strategy space would not establish optimal measured throughput. Section 3.5's fixed-time solver argument bounds a truncated procedure, not the complexity of finding an optimal solution.

The experiments do not isolate the central claim that joint optimization explains the improvements over hierarchical approaches. Figure 7 compares against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only variants, rather than a hierarchical optimizer using the same candidates and cost model. Hierarchical decomposition does not inherently imply suboptimality. Differences in cost-model accuracy, supported strategies, frameworks, and solver threading leave the source of the gains insufficiently established.

Memory feasibility is insufficiently specified and validated. Algorithm 1 constructs memory costs using micro-batch size b=B/c, but the description does not explain how retained activations across GPipe micro-batches are accounted for when checkpointing is disabled. Figure 7 also reports CUDA OOM for the intra-layer-only UniAP variant despite the memory constraint. Throughput-prediction accuracy at selected solutions does not validate peak-memory estimates or candidate ranking.

The practical results are worthwhile, but they do not resolve the central formulation and optimality concerns, which determine my weak-reject recommendation. Secondary limitations include scaling only to 16 GPUs, predominantly FP32 experiments without checkpointing, and optimization timings that exclude profiling; these restrict the demonstrated applicability and end-to-end setup benefit.
